c.tagline: Bohemian English seaside city famous for its pier, Regency architecture, and LGBTQ+-friendly nightlife.

taxi.fareNote: Licensed black cabs and private hire minicabs run on metered or pre-agreed fares; Uber is widely available.

emergency.note: Dial 999 for police, fire, or ambulance in a genuine emergency; 101 for non-emergency police and 111 for NHS non-emergency medical advice.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: West Street and the seafront club strip get rowdy with drunken crowds late on weekend nights.

hood_desc: A maze of narrow medieval alleyways in the old fishing quarter, now packed with jewelers, antique shops, and cafes, with the Royal Pavilion just to the north.
Brighton's bohemian shopping district, full of independent boutiques, vintage stores, vegan cafes, and street art near the station-to-seafront axis.
The heart of Brighton's LGBTQ+ scene along St James's Street, with a dense cluster of bars, clubs, and drag venues alongside elegant Regency squares.
Brighton's more genteel western neighbor, with grand Regency terraces, wide lawns along the seafront, and a calmer pace than the city center.
The promenade running from the Palace Pier to the i360 tower, with the beach, arcades, and the burnt-out skeleton of the old West Pier.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the UK.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5am-midnight with some night services on key routes; trains run until around midnight
transit.pay: Contactless bank card, the Brighton & Hove Buses app, or PayPoint travel cards
transit.note: No underground or metro; buses and trains cover the city and region, and the center itself is very walkable and bikeable.

train: Direct trains to London Victoria and London St Pancras International (about 1 hour), plus coastal lines to Portsmouth, Hastings, and Southampton
bus: National Express coaches to London and regional towns

car.idp: Not required for short US/EU visits

tip.r: A 10-12.5% service charge is often added automatically at restaurants; tipping taxis or bars isn't expected, though rounding up is common.

food.name: Fish and chips
food.desc: Beer-battered cod or haddock with thick chips, mushy peas and vinegar, best eaten from paper on the pebbles while gulls plot overhead.

places.name: Bardsley's
places.note: A Brighton chippy since the 1920s; proper licensed sit-down restaurant, generous portions.

places.name: Captain's Fish and Chips
places.note: Open since 1990, right on the seafront with a view of the shoreline.

places.name: The Regency Restaurant
places.note: Long-standing seafront institution for classic fish and chips and seafood.

food.name: Seafood on the beach
food.desc: Oysters, cockles, whelks, jellied eels and smoked mackerel eaten straight from the arches by the old fishing quarter, no tablecloth required.

places.name: English's of Brighton
places.note: Eighty-odd years of oysters and shellfish in the same converted fishermen's cottages.

places.name: Jack and Linda Trotter's Smokehouse
places.note: Beach hut run by former fishing folk; smoked mackerel and fish soup on the pebbles.

places.name: Brighton Smokehouse
places.note: Smokes and cures its own fish on site, eaten at benches facing the sea.

food.name: Sussex crab and day-boat small plates
food.desc: Brown crab, Rye Bay scallops and line-caught bass from the Sussex coast, served as sharing plates rather than a plated main.

places.name: Riddle and Finns
places.note: Champagne-and-oyster bar with two branches; marble counters and daily catch boards.

places.name: The Salt Room
places.note: Coal-grill seafood facing the West Pier ruins; strong on whole fish and crab.

places.name: English's of Brighton
places.note: Dressed crab and native oysters from the city's oldest seafood house.

food.name: Vegan fish and chips and plant-based cooking
food.desc: Brighton is repeatedly named the UK's most vegan city; banana-blossom fish, tofish and vegan pizza are mainstream here, not novelty.

places.name: No Catch
places.note: Fully vegan chippy using banana blossom to mimic flaky white fish.

places.name: Purezza
places.note: Britain's first vegan pizzeria, still one of the best-regarded plant-based kitchens in town.

places.name: Oowee Vegan
places.note: Loud, cheap plant-based junk food including vegan fish and chips and loaded fries.

food.name: Doughnuts on the pier
food.desc: Bags of hot ring doughnuts rolled in sugar, fried to order in the kiosks along Palace Pier. A Brighton seaside rite of passage.

places.name: Brighton Palace Pier doughnut kiosks
places.note: Fried fresh in front of you; buy a bag and eat them before you reach the end of the boards.

places.name: Sugardough
places.note: Independent bakery whose filled doughnuts and pastries have a loyal local following.

places.name: The Flour Pot Bakery
places.note: Excellent doughnuts, buns and coffee a few minutes from the seafront.

food.name: Seaside gelato and ice cream
food.desc: The promenade ice cream habit, upgraded by a cluster of independent gelaterias making small batches with local milk and odd flavours.

places.name: Boho Gelato
places.note: Cult gelateria with a rotating board of inventive flavours near the seafront.

places.name: Marrocco's
places.note: Family Italian ice cream parlour on Hove seafront, going for decades.

places.name: Gelato Gusto
places.note: Made on the premises daily; good vegan sorbets alongside the dairy gelato.

food.name: Sussex ale
food.desc: Harvey's Sussex Best and other county bitters, served by gravity or handpump in Brighton's back-street pubs.

places.name: The Basketmakers Arms
places.note: Beloved backstreet pub, tins on the walls, consistently well-kept ale.

places.name: The Evening Star
places.note: The pub where Dark Star Brewing began; still a serious real-ale destination.

places.name: The Lion and Lobster
places.note: Rambling multi-floor pub with a roof terrace and a strong cask list.

food.name: Sussex sparkling wine
food.desc: The South Downs chalk grows the same grapes as Champagne; Sussex fizz from Ridgeview, Rathfinny and Bolney is now a genuine local drink.

places.name: Riddle and Finns
places.note: Oyster bar with a proper English sparkling list by the glass.

places.name: Plateau
places.note: Natural and low-intervention wine bar that champions English producers.

places.name: The Salt Room
places.note: Sussex fizz with sea views over the West Pier.

landmarks: Royal Pavilion
George IV's outrageous seaside palace piles Indian domes and minarets over opulent Chinese-inspired interiors, the most exotic royal residence in Britain.
Brighton Palace Pier
The quintessential Victorian pleasure pier juts 524 meters over the Channel, packed with arcades, fairground rides, doughnut stalls and squawking gulls.
The Lanes
A labyrinth of narrow seventeenth-century fishing-village alleys now crammed with jewelers, antique dealers and pubs, perfect for aimless treasure-hunt wandering.
British Airways i360
Marks Barfield's 162-meter observation tower lifts a glass doughnut pod above the seafront for views along the Sussex coast and South Downs.
Brighton Beach and Seafront
Four miles of pebbles, striped deckchairs, artist studios in the arches and sunset crowds define England's most exuberant urban seaside promenade.
North Laine
Brighton's bohemian quarter packs over 300 independent shops, vegan cafes, record stores and street art into a few gloriously nonconformist blocks.
West Pier Ruins
The skeletal iron remains of the 1866 West Pier stand marooned offshore, a hauntingly beautiful roost for Brighton's swirling starling murmurations.
Sea Life Brighton
The world's oldest operating aquarium, opened in 1872, retains its Victorian arcaded hall while sharks and turtles cruise a modern ocean tunnel.
Brighton Museum and Art Gallery
Set in the Royal Pavilion's gardens, this eclectic museum spans Art Deco furniture, world cultures and irreverent exhibits on Brighton's seaside history.
Volk's Electric Railway
The world's oldest operating electric railway, running along Brighton's seafront since 1883 between the Aquarium and Black Rock in vintage open-sided carriages.

train.note: No international trains from Brighton, though the connection is easier than most: Thameslink runs direct to London St Pancras for Eurostar in about 1h20 without changing stations. Southern services reach London Victoria in an hour and run along the coast to Lewes, Eastbourne and Portsmouth. The station is a ten-minute walk downhill to the seafront. Advance fares open 12 weeks out.

bus.note: No direct international coaches. National Express (https://www.nationalexpress.com/) runs from Pool Valley coach station to London Victoria in about 2h30 and direct to Gatwick in 45 minutes and Heathrow in 2 hours, which is the usual reason to take the coach here.

intl.to: Dieppe (France) - sails from Newhaven, ~15 km east of Brighton, ~4 hr

ferry.note: Brighton itself has only a marina, but Newhaven, 15 minutes east by train, has the shortest crossing to Normandy: DFDS sails to Dieppe twice a day year-round, taking about four hours. It carries cars and foot passengers, and Dieppe has onward rail to Rouen and Paris. Bring your passport, and note that foot-passenger access at Newhaven is more awkward than at Dover.

half.name: Devil's Dyke
half.blurb: A short bus ride into the South Downs, Britain's deepest dry valley unfurls hang-gliders and hundred-kilometer views over the Weald.
